c: is an interior and graphic design aesthetic that became popular among Gen Z in the 2020s, specifically on TikTok, and later Instagram and Pinterest. It is characterized by having pastel,

furniture and accessories against naturally lit white rooms. Like other TikTok interior design aesthetics, certain products and designs have become iconic and are featured in almost every iteration of the aesthetic. For Danish Pastel, those products are wavy, organically-shaped candles and mirrors, milk crate storage boxes, and checkerboard rugs, all in the styles' signature pastel color palette.
This aesthetic arose as a direct response to both the widespread minimalist trend of the 2010s as well as the COVID-19 lockdown of 2020. The 2010s saw the rise of

, and with that, a cultural design shift towards simple, sophisticated interiors, industrial accents, and neutral-to-beige color palettes. Generation Z systemically rejected this, finding it restrictive, and embraced all things
instead, in both fashion and interior design. This can be seen in the bold color combinations, eye-catching patterns, and asymmetrical, often cluttered, decorations.

Danish Pastel was also a result of the global lockdowns of 2020 caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Many sought to redesign their interior spaces due to being constantly confined to them, and desired a more optimistic, comforting design style to counter the chaos of the world outside. For some, bringing colors like bright blue and soft yellow into the home was an attempt to re-experience the beauty of nature that was being withheld from them due to the lockdown.
Much of this aesthetic takes inspiration from modern art that emphasizes shapes in flat colors, such as works by Matisse and Picasso.

Danish Pastel prioritizes pairing fun, childlike, and abstract elements with Scandi and Scandi-inspired furniture. It overtly emphasizes a bright pastel color palette, but also highlights whimsy by mixing patterns and including organic shapes wherever possible. Decorative elements such as pillows, vases, candles, and mirror frames are often characterized by playful, fluid forms. These organic forms contrast with the rigidity of the patterns often found in this style. Likewise, checkerboard, stripes, and grid patterns dominate this aesthetic, adding structure to the otherwise soft sensibilities of the trend.

Of course, pastels are the focal point of the aesthetic. These are typically bright or "neon" pastels rather than pale ones, with the most common colors being pink, lilac, baby blue, soft yellow, green, and white. Though it can go in a more minimalist direction, the trend encourages lots of layered decor in the home, often mixing colors and prints recklessly. Gallery walls, bookshelves lined with books and trinkets, and floating scalloped shelves topped with vases and plants are common sights in the Danish Pastel home. Critics of Danish Pastel dislike the trends' "cute-ification" of its sophisticated predecessor, Scandinavian design, and say it removes the intentional complexity and depth of the style in favor of trendy childlike colors and imagery. Some say there is more Japanese influence in this aesthetic than Scandinavian, and very little Danish design included at all, expressing confusion over the name of the aesthetic.
